```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Problem 1

```{r load-penguins}
data("penguins", package = "palmerpenguins")
```

The penguins dataset contains measurements of penguins from the Palmer Archipelago in Antarctica. It has `r nrow(penguins)` rows and `r ncol(penguins)` columns. Important variables include species (`r paste(levels(penguins$species), collapse = ", ")`), island (`r paste(levels(penguins$island), collapse = ", ")`), bill length and depth (mm), flipper length (mm), body mass (g), sex, and year.

The mean flipper length is `r round(mean(penguins$flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` mm, excluding missing values.

```{r penguin-scatterplot}
penguin_plot = ggplot(
  penguins,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = flipper_length_mm, color = species)
) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Flipper length versus bill length",
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Flipper length (mm)",
    color = "Species"
  )

penguin_plot

ggsave(
  filename = "penguin_scatterplot.png",
  plot = penguin_plot,
  width = 7,
  height = 5,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 300
)
```

The scatterplot shows the relationship between bill length and flipper length, with different colors representing the three penguin species. Penguins with missing measurements are omitted from the plot.



## Problem 2

```{r create-dataframe}
set.seed(123)

variable_types = tibble(
  normal_sample = rnorm(10),
  is_positive = normal_sample > 0,
  character_values = c(
    "apple", "banana", "cherry", "apple", "banana",
    "cherry", "apple", "banana", "cherry", "apple"
  ),
  factor_values = factor(
    c("low", "medium", "high", "low", "medium",
      "high", "low", "medium", "high", "low"),
    levels = c("low", "medium", "high")
  )
)

variable_types
```

This data frame contains a random sample of 10 values from a standard Normal distribution, a logical variable indicating whether each value is greater than zero, a character variable, and a factor with three levels: low, medium, and high. Setting a seed makes the random sample reproducible.

```{r calculate-means}
mean(pull(variable_types, normal_sample))
mean(pull(variable_types, is_positive))
mean(pull(variable_types, character_values))
mean(pull(variable_types, factor_values))
```

The mean of the numeric sample is `r round(mean(pull(variable_types, normal_sample)), 3)`. The mean of the logical variable is `r mean(pull(variable_types, is_positive))`, which is the proportion of sample values greater than zero. R treats TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 when calculating this mean.

The character and factor variables both return NA with warnings when passed directly to mean(), because these types are not accepted as numeric inputs by mean().

```{r numeric-coercion, results='hide', warning=FALSE}
as.numeric(pull(variable_types, is_positive))
as.numeric(pull(variable_types, character_values))
as.numeric(pull(variable_types, factor_values))
```

Converting the logical variable to numeric produces 1 for TRUE and 0 for FALSE. This explains why its mean can be calculated directly.

Converting the character variable produces NA values and a warning because the fruit names cannot be interpreted as numbers.

Converting the factor produces its internal integer codes: 1 for low, 2 for medium, and 3 for high, following the specified level order. These codes represent categories rather than measured quantities. Although their mean could be calculated after conversion, it would not be a meaningful average of the categories. The original factor cannot be averaged directly.
